Abstract

The phase field approach is a powerful and popular method for modeling microstructure evolution. In this work, advanced numerical tools are used to create a framework that facilitates rapid model development. This framework, called MARMOT, is based on Idaho National Laboratory’s finite element Multiphysics Object-Oriented Simulation Environment. In MARMOT, the system of phase field partial differential equations (PDEs) are solved simultaneously together with PDEs describing additional physics, such as solid mechanics and heat conduction, using the Jacobian-Free Newton Krylov Method. An object-oriented architecture is created by taking advantage of commonalities in the phase field PDEs to facilitate development of new models with very little effort. In addition, MARMOT provides access to mesh and time step adaptivity, reducing the cost for performing simulations with large disparities in both spatial and temporal scales. In this work, phase separation simulations are used to show the numerical performance of MARMOT. Deformation-induced grain growth and void growth simulations are also included to demonstrate the muliphysics capability.

Highlights

▸ Generic phase field framework created using advanced computational tools. ▸ Multiphysics phase field equations are solved fully coupled using JFNK. ▸ Object-oriented architecture is used to facilitate development of new models. ▸ Mesh adaptivity used to accurately resolve interfacial widths. ▸ Time step is adapted to follow evolving time scale.

1. Introduction

Over the past 20 years the phase field approach has become a popular and powerful tool to model microstructure evolution. Due to its simple concept and large range of applicability, it has been used to model various physical phenomena including grain boundary migration, martinsitic transformation, dislocation motion and two phase flow [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. In the phase field approach, microstructural features are represented with continuous variables that smoothly transition from one value to another, thus all material interfaces are treated as diffuse. This description of the interfaces eliminates the need to explicitly discretize a boundary or interface. In addition, the phase field model is deterministic, with partial differential equations (PDEs) defining the evolution of the continuous variables that describe the microstructure.
The majority of phase field papers in the literature focus on model development and not on the numerical architecture used to solve the system of equations. However, a large range of different numerical techniques have been applied. Most authors use finite difference approximations [6], [7] or spectral methods that employ the fast Fourier Transform [8], [9], [10], though some have employed the finite element method (FEM) [11], [12]. Many authors use serial codes and explicit time integration schemes.
In this work, we demonstrate how various numerical tools can be used to create a phase field framework which allows rapid development of advanced phase field models. This framework, which we call MARMOT, is built using Idaho National Laboratory’s (INL’s) Multiphysics Object-Oriented Simulation Environment, or MOOSE [13]. MOOSE is a massively parallel finite element-based system to solve large systems of equations using the Jacobian-Free Newton Krylov (JFNK) method. An object-oriented architecture is employed to minimize the programming required to develop a phase field model and to maximize code reuse. Within MARMOT, the phase field equations can be easily coupled to additional physics, such as solid mechanics or heat conduction, to add additional driving forces for microstructure evolution. In addition, time step and mesh adaptivity can be used to reduce the computational cost.
MOOSE and MARMOT are both intrinsic parts of the Fuel Cycle Research and Development Program’s fuel performance code, M-B-M (MOOSE-BISON-MARMOT). M-B-M is a multiscale fuel performance code for modeling LWR, TRISO, and plate fuels, as well as next generation fuel concepts. It is also leading the fuel performance modeling efforts of the Nuclear Energy Advanced Modeling and Simulation program and the Consortium of Advanced Simulation of Light Water Reactors.
In this paper, we begin in Section 2 by describing the finite element solution of the phase field equations using JFNK. In Section 3, we demonstrate how object-oriented programming can be employed to simplify phase field model development. Finally, in Section 4 we apply the MARMOT framework to solve three distinct phase field models demonstrating the benefits of various features of the framework.

2. Finite element formulation

In the phase field approach, microstructural features are described using continuous variables. These variables take two forms: conserved variables representing physical properties such as atom concentration or material density, and nonconserved order parameters describing the microstructure of the material, including grains and different phases. The evolution of these continuous variables is a function of the Gibbs free energy and can be defined as a system of PDEs.
In Chen [5], a general form of the phase field PDEs is defined. We present this general form here, and then show how it can be solved via FEM. The evolution of all conserved variables is defined using modified Cahn–Hilliard equations, i.e.(1)𝜕𝑐𝑖𝜕𝑡=𝛻·𝑀𝑖𝛻𝜕𝐹𝜕𝑐𝑖,where ci is a conserved variable and Mi is the associated mobility. The evolution of nonconserved order parameters is represented with an Allen–Cahn equation, according to(2)𝜕𝜂𝑗𝜕𝑡=−𝐿𝑗⁢𝜕𝐹𝜕𝜂𝑗,where ηj is an order parameter and Lj is the order parameter mobility. The Gibbs free energy of the system is defined by the functional F.
The free energy functional, for a phase field model using N conserved variables ci and M order parameters ηj, is described by(3)𝐹=∫𝑉[𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐⁡(𝑐1,…,𝑐𝑁,𝜂1,…,𝜂𝑀)+𝑓𝑔𝑟⁡(𝑐1,…,𝑐𝑁,𝜂1,…,𝜂𝑀)+𝐸𝑑]𝑑𝑉,where floc defines the local free energy density as a function of all concentrations and order parameters. The gradient energy density(4)𝑓𝑔𝑟=𝑁∑𝑖𝜅𝑖2⁢|𝛻𝑐𝑖|2+𝑀∑𝑗𝜅𝑗2⁢|𝛻𝜂𝑗|2,where κi and κj are gradient energy coefficients. Finally, Ed describes any additional sources of energy in the system, such as deformation or electrostatic energy. By substituting Eq. (4) into Eqs. (1), (2), the evolution of the variables is described as(5)𝜕𝑐𝑖𝜕𝑡=𝛻·𝑀𝑖𝛻(𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝑐𝑖−𝜅𝑖𝛻2𝑐𝑖+𝜕𝐸𝑑𝜕𝑐𝑖)(6)𝜕𝜂𝑗𝜕𝑡=−𝐿⁢(𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝜂𝑗−𝜅𝑗𝛻2𝜂𝑗+𝜕𝐸𝑑𝜕𝜂𝑗).
To prepare for the FEM discretization of Eqs. (5), (6), we construct a weak form in a similar manner to that used by Stogner et al. [14]. First, the weighted integral residual projection of Eqs. (5), (6) is constructed using test function ϕm and integrating the second-order terms by parts once and the fourth order term by parts twice. Thus, Eq. (5) yields(7)(𝜕𝑐𝑖𝜕𝑡,𝜙𝑚)=−(𝜅𝑖𝛻2𝑐𝑖,𝛻·(𝑀𝑖𝛻𝜙𝑚))−(𝑀𝑖𝛻(𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝑐𝑖+𝜕𝐸𝑑𝜕𝑐𝑖),𝛻𝜙𝑚)+⟨𝑀𝑖𝛻(𝜅𝑖𝛻2𝑐𝑖)·→𝑛,𝜙𝑚⟩−⟨𝑀𝑖𝛻(𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝑐𝑖+𝜕𝐸𝑑𝜕𝑐𝑖)·→𝑛,𝜙𝑚⟩+⟨𝜅𝑖𝛻2𝑐𝑖,𝑀𝑖𝛻𝜙𝑚·→𝑛⟩,where the usual inner product notation is used for the respective interior and boundary integrals. Eq. (6) yields(8)(𝜕𝜂𝑗𝜕𝑡,𝜙𝑚)=−𝐿⁡(𝜅𝑗𝛻𝜂𝑗,𝛻𝜙𝑚)−𝐿⁡(𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝜂𝑗+𝜕𝐸𝑑𝜕𝜂𝑗,𝜙𝑚)+𝐿⁡〈𝜅𝑗𝛻𝜂𝑗·→𝑛,𝜙𝑚〉.The weak statement is completed with an initial condition and boundary conditions. For the Cahn–Hilliard equation, natural boundary conditions can be applied via the penalty method discussed in Stogner et al. [14].
When additional physics are coupled to the phase field equations, additional residual equations are solved, e.g. coupling to a solid mechanics solution would require the residual equation(9)(𝜌⁢𝜕2𝐮𝜕𝑡2,𝜙𝑚)=(𝝈⁡(𝐮),𝛻𝜙𝑚))−〈𝜎⁡(𝐮)·→𝑛,𝜙𝑚〉,where the stress tensor σ is a function of the displacements u and ρ is the density. Coupling to heat conduction to determine the temperature T would require the equation(10)(𝜌⁢𝑐𝑝⁢𝜕𝑇𝜕𝑡,𝜙𝑚)=(𝑘𝛻𝑇,𝛻𝜙𝑚)−〈𝑘𝛻𝑇·→𝑛,𝜙𝑚〉,where cp is the specific heat and k is the thermal conductivity.
Each equation is discretized in the typical FEM manner, and all of the required FEM objects and architecture are provided by MOOSE. Cubic C1 Hermite elements are used to discretize the conserved variables while linear Lagrange elements are used for the order parameters and any coupled variables such as displacements or temperature. The transient system of PDEs is integrated over time implicitly. The system of coupled PDEs defined by Eqs. (7), (8), (9), (10) is solved with JFNK in the manner described in Gaston et al. [13]. We have found that diagonal block preconditioning is sufficient for most systems, therefore only an approximation of the diagonal blocks of the Jacobian of each residual with its corresponding variable need be determined.

3. Object-oriented framework

The goal of the MARMOT framework is to facilitate the development of advanced phase field models by taking advantage of their common structure, i.e. their usage of Eqs. (7), (8). Thus, only the terms ∇∂ floc/∂ci, ∇∂Ed/∂ci, ∂ floc/∂ηj, ∂Ed/∂ηj, and the parameters Mi, κi, Lj and κj vary between models. By employing object-oriented design principles, the development of a new phase field model using MARMOT only requires that the behavior of these varying terms be defined. In this way, even complex phase field models can be created with only small amounts of effort. This small amount of required effort is accomplished by dividing up the residual equations into several separate terms. Each of these terms has been created as a C++ base class, with interfaces for the required terms. Therefore, creating a new phase field model is accomplished by inheriting from these base classes and overriding functions to provide the specific free energy terms and model parameters.
For example, the interior terms of Eq. (7) can be divided into four pieces, the time derivative, the gradient term, the local energy term and the additional energy term, as shown in Table 1. A base class has been created for each of these four terms. The gradient energy class requires the parameters ki and Mi to be defined but has no functions to be overridden. The local energy class requires Mi be defined and the function ∇ ∂floc/∂ci be overridden; the additional energy class requires Mi and that ∇∂Ed/∂ci be overridden. Thus, to define the residual for a conserved variable, a material object is created supplying κi and Mi, as are objects inheriting from the local energy and additional energy classes, overriding the necessary functions. This process is repeated for all of the conserved variables required by the model, though often their forms are similar and code can be reused. A similar process is followed for all the order parameters and any other coupled variables, such as displacements and temperature. Commonly used terms, such as the time derivative or a scalar forcing function already exist in MOOSE and can be used without additional coding.

MARMOT is fully parallel, as are all MOOSE-based applications. This capability is provided without requiring MPI calls or any other parallel considerations. The parallel scalability is near ideal, as shown in Section 4 below.
MARMOT also provides the ability to adapt the mesh and the time step in order to reduce the computational cost of the solution. These capabilities do not require any development by the user, but already exist in MOOSE and are easily accessed through the input file. By adapting the time step, the evolving time scale of the problem can be followed as the microstructure evolves. Two adaptive time step algorithms are discussed in the following section.
Mesh adaptivity changes the mesh after each time step to concentrate the degrees of freedom of the system where they are needed to better capture the solution. This is especially applicable to the phase field technique due to the diffuse interface representation [15], [11], [16]. Typically, a fine resolution is required to capture the evolution at the interface, but a much coarser resolution can be used to resolve the bulk material. The mesh adaptivity is based on an error indicator, many of which exist in the literature. The mesh adaptivity algorithm used in MOOSE is described in Stogner et al. [14]. Both mesh and time step adaptivity are powerful tools for the phase field technique since they allow for the description of multiple scales throughout a single simulation.

4. MARMOT examples

To demonstrate the capabilities of MARMOT, we use three example problems. The first example is simple spinodal decomposition, which we use to demonstrate the numerical performance of MARMOT. The second example is a grain growth simulation of copper polycrystals, including an elastically-deformed polycrystal. Finally, for the third example we model the effect of irradiation-induced void growth on thermal conductivity.

4.1. Spinodal decomposition

To investigate the numerical performance of the MARMOT framework, we use a phase-separation model of spinodal decomposition in an isothermal binary system. A single concentration variable c is used to represent the two phases of the binary system and the time evolution is defined with a single Cahn–Hilliard equation (Eq. (7)). The phase separation behavior is defined with the common double well free energy function(11)𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐=14⁢(1−𝑐2)⁢2.Therefore, a local energy object is created that satisfies the required interface(12)𝛻𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝑐=(3⁢𝑐2−1)𝛻𝑐.We assume a constant mobility M = 1, and a constant gradient coefficient κi = 0.3 and the time integration in the system is carried out using the Crank–Nicolson method.
We first demonstrate the parallel scalability of MARMOT on a 2-D domain using a C1 continuous cross initial condition (see Fig. 1a). A mesh with 200 × 200 elements is used, giving 161,604 degrees of freedom (DOFs). Ten time steps of dt = 2.0 × 10−6 are taken and the computation is completed using from one to twelve 2.93 GHz Intel Nehalem processors. Our results show that the scaling begins to deviate from ideal below 20,000 DOF per processor, as shown in Fig. 2b.
Next, we simulate spinodal decomposition using a random initial condition. Stogner et al. [14] showed that when resolving a purely random initial condition, a very small initial time step is required to avoid large error in the implicit integration. While using a constant time step of this small magnitude would be infeasible, time step adaptivity based on an integration error estimate allows the time step to grow and still maintain low integration error. We employ the same adaptive time stepping scheme as used in Stogner et al. [14], and we summarize it here.
To estimate the time integration error, time is advanced from time tn to tn+1 in two ways; one time step of size dt is taken to compute cn+1 from cn and two steps of size dt/2 are also taken to compute ̂𝑐𝑛+1. The relative time discretization error is estimated according to(13)𝑒𝑛≡1𝑑𝑡⁢‖𝑐𝑛+1−̂𝑐𝑛+1‖𝑚𝑎𝑥⁡(𝑐𝑛+1,̂𝑐𝑛+1).Note that while this method provides an estimate of the integration error, it requires three solutions of the system of equations for every one time step. The time step adaptivity is based on a target error tolerance etol and a maximum increase per time step. The next time step is determined according to(14)𝑑𝑡𝑛+1=𝑑𝑡𝑛⁢(𝑒𝑡𝑜𝑙𝑒𝑛)1/𝑝where p is the global convergence rate of the time stepping algorithm being used; e.g. p = 2 for Crank–Nicolson. If the computed time step exceeds the maximum increase per time step, a value equal to the maximum is used.
Though the time step required to model the random initial condition is very small, a larger time step can be used as the phase separation progresses. Fig. 2 shows several stages of phase separation in a 3-D domain and also shows a plot of time step size vs nondimensional time. The time step begins at 1 × 10−4 and it steadily increases until it is above 10, after which time it fluctuates, as it attempts to take large time steps for which the nonlinear system will not converge. The maximum time step taken is 45. The adaptive time step algorithm was used with etol = 0.1 and a maximum increase of 10%. It reached t = 3000 in 242 steps. This behavior is consistent with results from a 2-D simulation of spinodal decomposition by Stogner et al. [14].
Time step and mesh adaptivity allow the computational expense to be concentrated where it is most needed in both space and time. However, there is an associated cost with using these methods that for some problems would eliminate any benefit. In addition, some error is associated with adapting both spatially and in time.
Now, we use the spinodal decomposition problem to investigate the total computation time and error resulting from adapting the mesh and the time step. To allow a larger initial time step than is required for a purely random initial condition, we initially evolved a random initial condition to a time of 0.6, at which time the integration error associated with a time step of 0.1 is below 0.5. Starting from this evolved microstructure, the phase separation is modeled with a constant time step of 0.1 and a constant 160 × 160 uniform mesh to a time of t = 3000, as the benchmark case. We also run three other simulations, one in which only the time step is adapted (etol = 0.5 and max increase of 10%), one in which only the mesh is adapted and finally one in which both the time step and mesh are adapted. To compare the accuracy of the solution, we compute a scalar value via a horizontal line integral across the domain and one via a vertical line integral. These scalar values are compared to similar scalar line integral values computed in the benchmark case. The line integrals provide a means of comparing the solution with varying time steps and meshes. We estimate the integral error for a specific simulation fa by comparing to the benchmark solution f0 according to eint = ∣f0 − fa∣/ max(∣fa∣) and combine the horizontal and vertical integral errors with a root mean square.
The four simulations predicted similar microstructures, as shown in Fig. 3a. By adapting the time step, the computation time was reduced by 80% from the time required by the simulation with no adaptivity (see Fig. 3b); mesh adaptivity reduced the computation time by 20%; both time step and mesh adaptivity reduced the computation time by 90%. The simulation errors vary significantly throughout the simulation, since it is measured along one horizontal and one vertical line. The error in the simulation using time step adaptivity varies from less then 0.1% error to 1.5% error, with an average error of 0.27% (Fig. 3c). The mesh adaptivity simulation resulted in an error with a maximum of 2.0% and has an average value of 0.4%. The simulation with both time step and mesh adaptivity reached 1.3%, with an average of 0.39%. In the two simulations in which the time step was adapted, the time step ranged from the initial value of 0.1 to a value of 65 in the simulation using just time step adaptivity and 95 in the simulation that used both types of adaptivity (Fig. 3d). The simulation using only mesh adaptivity reduced the number of degrees of freedom (DOF) from 10,200 to 4200, though the savings in computation time was only 20% (Fig. 3e). The simulation using both mesh and time adaptivity reduced the number of DOFs rapidly when the time steps were small, but once it began to take large time steps, the mesh did not adapt as efficiently and the number of DOFs went up.
By using both mesh and time step adaptivity to solve the spinodal decomposition simulation, the computation time was reduced by a factor of 10 with an associated average error of only 0.39%. Time step adaptivity alone reduced the computation time by a factor of five with an error of 0.27%. In the simulation using mesh adaptivity, the number of DOF was reduced by a factor of 2.3 but the computational cost was only reduced by 20%. This small reduction in computation cost is due in part to the associated cost of adapting the mesh 30,000 times and also due to parallel overhead cost as the number of DOFs per processor gradually decreases.

4.2. Grain growth

For the next example of MARMOT’s capabilities, we model grain growth in copper polycrystals using the phase field formulation presented in Moelans et al. [17]. We also show the effect of an applied deformation on grain growth using the model discussed in Tonks et al. [18] and Tonks and Millett [19].
In this phase field grain growth model, each grain is represented by a continuous order parameter ηi equal to one within the grain and zero in all other grains. The evolution of each grain’s order parameter is defined with Eq. (8). A local energy object is created, in which(15)𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝜂𝑖=𝜇⁢⎛⎜ ⎜⎝𝜂3𝑖−𝜂𝑖+2⁢𝑁∑𝑗≠1𝜂𝑖⁢𝜂2𝑗⎞⎟ ⎟⎠.Since this equation takes the same form for each order parameter, only one object is created and reused for each order parameter.
In Moelans et al. [17], the model parameters Lj, μ and κj are defined in terms of the grain boundary (GB) surface energy σ, the diffuse GB width wGB and the GB mobility mGB. Tonks et al. [18] and Tonks and Millett [19] quantify the model for pure copper from properties measured with molecular dynamics simulation in Schönfelder et al. [20], i.e. σ = 0.708 J/m2 and 𝑚𝐺𝐵=𝑚0⁢exp⁡(−𝑄𝑘𝐵⁢𝑇), where kB is the Boltzmann constant, T is the absolute temperature, m0 = 2.5  × 10−6 m4/(Js) and Q = 0.23 eV, and we use the same properties here. The diffuse GB width is typically taken as the largest value that does not effect the results at a specific descretized grid spacing. Tonks et al. [18] found the best value for a grid spacing of 10 nm to be wGB = 45 nm.
An applied elastic deformation contributes to the free energy of the system and thus effects the grain boundary migration. In this work we only apply small deformations and assume linear elasticity accurately describes the material behavior such that 𝝈=𝓒⁢𝛆. The polycrystal elasticity tensor 𝓒 is a function of the order parameters according to(16)𝓒⁡(𝜂1,𝜂2,…,𝜂𝑁)=∑𝑁𝑖ℎ⁡(𝜂𝑖)⁢𝓒𝑖∑𝑁𝑖ℎ⁡(𝜂𝑖),where 𝓒𝑖 is the elastic tensor from the corresponding grain orientation and the smooth function h(ηi) =  (1 + sin (π(ηi − 1/2))/2. Since copper has a cubic crystal structure, the elastic tensor is fully defined by three temperature-dependent elastic constants [20](17)𝐶11=181.50−.109𝑇GPa𝐶12=101.80−.062𝑇GPa𝐶44=101.80−.057𝑇GPaTo define the contribution of the elastic energy to the residual equation, we create an additional energy block with(18)𝜕𝐸𝑑𝜕𝜂𝑖=12⁢(𝜕𝓒𝜕𝜂𝑖⁢𝛆)·𝛆In Tonks et al. [18] and Tonks and Millett [19], the phase field equations were solved using finite difference and the local strains were determined with a spectral method. The two solutions were operator split such that the strains were first calculated using the order parameters from the previous time step. Then, the order parameters were updated with the calculated strains. In MARMOT, the displacements are fully coupled to the phase field variables and they are all solved for simultaneously with FEM. In addition, due to the coupling and the implicit time integration, much larger time steps are taken in MARMOT than were used in the previous work.
The adaptive time step scheme discussed in the previous section guarantees the estimated integration error be below a set amount, however it requires three solutions of the system of equations for each time step. Thus, the scheme only decreases the overall computational expense if the time step consistently increases such that the overall number of time steps is reduced by more than three times, as was the case with spinodal decomposition (see Fig. 2). However, this is not the case in grain growth. Therefore, we use a different adaptive time step scheme based on the ratio of time step size to the CPU time required to solve the equation system. In the scheme, an initial adaptive direction is initially chosen, either increasing or decreasing the time step, and the time step is changed by 10% in that direction every time step. If the ratio decreases three time steps in a row, the direction switches. Once the direction switches, no changes are made to the time step for three additional steps. This scheme changes the time step in order to maximize the ratio of time step size to CPU time.
The GB width of wGB = 45 nm that was necessary with a fixed grid spacing of 10 nm is an order of magnitude larger than realistic GB widths. Capturing a more realistic GB width with a uniform grid would be computationally prohibitive. However, a more realistic GB width can be achieved using mesh adaptivity. In this demonstration, we compare the behavior predicted using a GB width of wGB = 45 nm to that predicted using a more realistic wGB = 5 nm (note that actual GB widths can be as small as 1 nm). We first compare the rate at which the grain area changes in simulations using the two GB widths. For this comparison, we simulate the shrinkage of a small circular grain imbedded within a much larger grain, using mesh adaptivity to lower the computation cost (see Fig. 4a for images of the simulation with the two GB widths). The GB velocity should be independent of GB width, therefore we compare the rate of change of the area of the circular grain with the two GB widths (see Fig. 4a for the mesh and GB configuration). We also conduct a 45 nm GB width simulation without mesh adaptivity to verify that the adaptivity is not effecting the grain growth. The three simulations predicted very similar rates of change of the grain area, as shown in Fig. 4b, verifying that the GB width does not effect the GB velocity and neither does mesh adaptivity.
Having established that the GB width does not effect the GB velocity, we now investigate its effect on the rate at which grains disappear. To evaluate the magnitude of this effect, we simulate the grain growth of a 4 μm × 4 μm square copper polycrystal with 35 grains. The boundaries on all four sides of the domain are treated as periodic. We observe the number of grains with time as the grains grow for 50 μs and we compare the results for GB widths of 45 nm and 5 nm. Note that the 5 nm GB width simulation has an average of four times as many DOFs as the 45 nm width simulation.
Fig. 5a shows the mesh for the two simulations with a larger magnitude view of the center of the mesh. Two additional levels of mesh refinement are needed to resolve the 5 nm GB width than the 45 nm width. The larger GB width does have a significant effect on the number of grains, as shown in Fig. 5b. The polycrystal with a GB width of 45 nm reaches 27 grains after 30 μs while the polycrystal with a 5 nm GB width does not reach 27 grains until after 42 μs. Both the difference in GB width and the differences in the microstructure can be clearly seen in images of the final polycrystals (see Fig. 5c). The GB width effects the rate at which grains disappear because it defines the amount of GB area in the polycrystal. Grains grow to minimize GB area, thus for larger GB width (and therefore more GB area) there is a larger driving force for grains to disappear.
It is also interesting to compare the time step size during the simulations. The time step size is typically lower for the 5 nm GB width polycrystal than the 45 nm width polycrysta, as shown in Fig. 5d. In addition, in both polycrystals a smaller time step is required to resolve the disappearance of a grain than is required to resolve only GB migration.
Finally, we simulate grain growth under an applied deformation. We consider a 4 μm × 2 μm 2-D copper polycrystal with 35 grains and a 5 nm GB width. The 35 grains are orientated randomly about the z-axis, such that all the GBs are symmetric tilt boundaries (see Fig. 6a for an image of the initial grain structure and the adapted mesh). For the grain order parameters, the top and bottom domain boundaries are periodic while the left and right have zero flux symmetric boundaries. The displacements are periodic on the top and bottom, they have a zero Dirichlet boundary in the x-and y-directions on the left surface, and the right surface is pulled 40 nm in the positive x-direction, corresponding to 1.0% strain. This load is maintained for 8.1 μs at a constant temperature of T = 450 K and the grains are allowed to grow freely.
The applied deformation modifies the grain growth kinetics, as shown in Fig. 6b. In addition, it causes the grains to grow anisotropically, with the grains oriented near 45°, which are harder with respect to the direction of the applied deformation, tending to shrink. Fig. 6c shows the microstructure after t = 8.1 μs in an undeformed and a deformed polycrystal. In the deformed polycrystal the grains shaded green (those oriented near 45°) have all reduced significantly in size, while the red grains (those oriented near 0°) have grown; there is no relationship between grain orientation and size in the undeformed polycrystal. The harder grains tend to have a higher stress (see Fig. 6d), such that the overall stored elastic energy in the polycrystal decreases with time (Fig. 6b). The continuous decrease in the elastic energy indicates that the energy decreases due to GB migration rather than the disappearance of grains. Thus, the phase field equations were fully-coupled to a linear elastic solid mechanics solution using JFNK with both mesh and time step adaptivity.

4.3. The effect of void formation on thermal conductivity

For the final demonstration of MARMOT, we simulate the effect of radiation damage on thermal conductivity in nuclear materials. In reactor applications, the effect of void formation on material thermal conductivity is important since the efficiency with which heat can be conducted to the coolant has a direct impact on energy generation. Voids form due to excess vacancies resulting from damage caused by neutron irradiation. The phase field approach has recently been used to model microstructure evolution due to radiation [21].
Rather than employ one of the previously suggested models, we employ a simplified representation of void formation and growth similar to phase separation. We define the free energy as a sixth order polynomial that has an energy minima at a vacancy concentration equal to the equilibrium concentration in the bulk, i.e. 𝑐𝑣=𝑐𝑒𝑞𝑣 and a minima at cv = 1 representing a void, as shown in Fig. 7a. Therefore, we create a local energy object with(19)𝛻𝜕𝑓𝑙𝑜𝑐𝜕𝑐𝑣=𝑊𝛻𝑐𝑣⁢(2⁢𝑐𝑣−1)⁢2⁢(𝑎𝑐2𝑣−𝑏𝑐𝑣+𝑐),where W defines the height of the energy barrier and(20)𝑎=54(21)𝑏=−54−𝑐𝑒𝑞𝑣(22)𝑐=1+7⁢𝑐𝑒𝑞𝑣8.For these simulations, we use values of 𝑐𝑒𝑞𝑣=1.0×10−4 and W = 100. The simulation is nondimensional in time, with a mobility Mi = 1.0 and gradient parameter κi = 1.0.
Representing the effect of radiation damage requires the addition of a stochastic vacancy source term to the residual Eq. (7), i.e. (Sv,ϕm). Sv is stochastic in both space and time to represent the clustering of excess vacancies that form around the location of a collision cascade. In reality, Frenkel pairs of interstitials and vacancies are created, with the vacancies centered at the collision location and the interstitials in a shell around the vacancies. However, to simplify the model used here, we only consider vacancies. A random number of collision cascades is determined at the start of each time step by sampling from a discrete normal distribution with mean of 3 and a standard deviation of 1. The collision locations of the N cascades that occur are randomly determined and the magnitude of Sv is calculated from a Cauchy distribution according to(23)𝑆𝑣⁡(𝐫)=𝑁∑𝑛1𝜋⁢𝛾‖𝐫−𝐫0𝑛‖+𝛾2where r is the current location and 𝐫0𝑛 is the nth collision location. Fig. 7b shows a plot of Sv over a 2-D domain. This function results in the vacancies being clustered around the collision location and is sufficiently smooth to ensure no convergence issues in the FEM solution. For this simulation, we use the value γ = π.
In Millett et al. [22] a heat conduction simulation is run concurrently with a phase field simulation of grain growth to determine the effect of grain growth and porosity on thermal conductivity. Similar simulations can be run over simulations of void formation and growth [23]. To determine the effective thermal conductivity, a steady-state heat conduction equation (see Eq. (10)) is solved over the domain, where the local thermal conductivity varies as a function of the vacancy concentration at the current position. In this work we use the expression(24)𝑘=(1−𝑐2𝑣)⁢𝑘𝑏𝑢𝑙𝑘+𝑐2𝑣⁢𝑘𝑣𝑜𝑖𝑑,where the thermal conductivity in the bulk of the material kbulk is determined from an expression for the thermal conductivity in UO2 [24], i.e.(25)𝑘bulk=1𝐶1+𝐶2⁢𝑇+𝐶3𝑇2⁢exp⁡(−𝐶4𝑇),with C1 = 0.0375 mK/W, C2 = 2.165 × 10−4 m/W, C3 = 4.715 × 109 WK/m and C4 = 16361 K. The void thermal conductivity is taken as that of He gas, kvoid = 0.152 W/m K. The heat conduction equation is solved with a fixed temperature boundary condition on the left side Tl = 800 K and a test heat flux 𝐪=𝑞𝑡̂𝐢 is applied over the right boundary. Periodic boundary conditions are applied over the top and bottom boundaries. The effective conductivity is determined with the expression(26)𝑘𝑒𝑓𝑓=−𝑞𝑡̅̅̅̅̅𝑇𝑟−𝑇𝑙𝑙,where ̅̅̅̅̅𝑇𝑟 the average temperature on the right boundary and l is the side length.
We consider a cube of material with sides of length 0.75 μm in which the vacancy concentration cv has zero flux symmetric boundary conditions on all sides. We take time steps of dt = 4 and calculate the effective thermal conductivity during each step. The heat conduction simulation is only used to probe the microstrcuture, such that cv effects T, but the evolution of cv is independent of T. Fig. 8a shows the final void structure along with isosurfaces showing the effect of the voids on the temperature profile in the material. After an initial nucleation period of t = 1000, voids begin to form resulting in a rapid increase in the porosity (see Fig. 8b). Once the nucleation of the voids is complete, the rate of increase of the porosity decreases slightly as the voids continue to grow. The effective thermal conductivity of the material slowly drops as the vacancy concentration increases in the material (Fig. 8c). However, once voids begin to form, the thermal conductivity begins to drop much faster. Once the voids stop nucleating and only grow, the drop in the thermal conductivity slows.
The above simulation was carried out by fully-coupling the solution of a phase field Cahn–Hilliard equation with a steady-state heat conduction equation in 3-D. Both linear Lagrange and third order Hermite elements were used in the simulation as was a stochastic vacancy source term.

5. Conclusions

Advanced numerical tools can be used to simplify implementation of the phase field approach, as illustrated with the MARMOT phase field framework. JFNK allows the system of phase field PDEs to be solved simultaneously and fully coupled with additional physics, including solid mechanics and heat conduction. Object-oriented design takes advantage of commonalities between phase field models to simplify development by only requiring the user to define the derivatives of the free energy functional. Mesh and time step adaptivity reduce computational cost while still resolving the necessary time and length scales.
In a phase separation simulation, mesh and time step adaptivity reduced the computational expense by a factor of 10 and only introduced an average error of 0.39%. In simulations of grain growth, mesh adaptivity facilitated the resolution of a 5 nm GB width, and it was shown that an overly large GB width, as is typically used in phase field grain growth simulations, accelerates the rate at which grains disappear. The multiphysics capability of MARMOT was demonstrated with a deformation-driven grain growth simulation and a simulation that predicted the effect of void growth on bulk thermal conductivity.
